HSA CONTRIBUTION LIMIT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How much can you put in your HSA in 2026?

The 2026 HSA contribution limit is $4,400 for self-only coverage or $8,750 for family coverage, plus a $1,000 catch-up at 55+. Only eligible for part of the year? This tool prorates the limit by month, or applies the last-month rule if you qualify — and explains the testing-period tradeoff that comes with it.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Coverage and eligibility

2. Optional: check your plan's HDHP qualification

Leave these blank to skip the qualification check and just compute the contribution limit.

Choose coverage type and eligible months, then click Calculate.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a full eligibility determination. This does not check for other disqualifying coverage — a general-purpose health FSA, Medicare enrollment, being claimed as a dependent, or a spouse's non-HDHP plan can eliminate HSA eligibility even during otherwise-eligible months.
  • Family limit is a household total, not per-spouse. If both spouses are HSA-eligible under family coverage, the $8,750 family limit is split between their two HSAs by agreement; this tool computes only the household total.
  • The catch-up cannot go into a spouse's HSA. A spouse who is 55+ and wants the catch-up contribution needs their own HSA in their own name.
  • Point-in-time 2026 figures. These limits are re-indexed annually (except the $1,000 catch-up, fixed by statute); confirm the current year's figures before relying on this in a later year.

Common questions

What is the 2026 HSA contribution limit?

$4,400 for self-only HDHP coverage or $8,750 for family coverage, per IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-19. Those 55 and older who are not yet enrolled in Medicare can contribute an additional $1,000 catch-up, which is fixed by statute rather than adjusted for inflation each year.

What deductible and out-of-pocket limits does a plan need to qualify as an HDHP in 2026?

The deductible must be at least $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage, and the out-of-pocket maximum must not exceed $8,500 for self-only or $17,000 for family. A plan outside these bounds is not HSA-qualified, whatever it is marketed as.

How is the HSA limit prorated if I was not covered all year?

By whole months of HDHP eligibility: the annual limit multiplied by eligible months divided by 12. Six months of self-only eligibility in 2026, for example, gives a prorated limit of $2,200 rather than the full $4,400.

What is the last-month rule, and what is the catch?

If you are HSA-eligible on December 1 of the tax year, you may contribute the full annual limit even if you were eligible for only part of the year. In exchange, you must remain HSA-eligible through December 31 of the following year (the testing period). If eligibility lapses before then for a reason other than death or disability, the amount you contributed beyond what proration would have allowed becomes taxable income in the year eligibility lapsed, plus a 10% additional tax.

Is this tax advice?

No. This tool applies published 2026 IRS figures to the numbers you enter. It does not check for other disqualifying coverage such as a general-purpose FSA, Medicare enrollment, or being claimed as a dependent, and it is not a substitute for IRS Publication 969 or a qualified tax professional.

This calculator vs. doing the HSA proration math by hand

Prorating a 2026 HSA contribution limit is arithmetic anyone can do with the right figures: the annual limit times eligible months over 12. The part a hand check most often gets wrong isn't the base limit -- it's remembering that the age-55 catch-up gets the same treatment, and that the last-month rule is a different election with its own separate condition, not just a bigger number.

Where a manual check usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake doing it by handWhat this calculator does
Prorating the age-55 catch-upAdding the full, unprorated $1,000 catch-up to a correctly prorated base limit, because the catch-up is fixed by statute and reads as a flat add-on rather than something that also scales with eligible months.Prorates the catch-up by the same eligible-months fraction as the base limit, unless the last-month rule applies.
Choosing proration vs. the last-month ruleTreating "I was eligible on December 1" as a bonus on top of the prorated amount rather than a full replacement of it, or reaching for it without checking eligibility on that specific date.Applies the last-month rule as an alternative to proration, only when you say you were (or will be) eligible on December 1, 2026.
Carrying the last-month rule's testing period forwardStopping at "I get the full limit this year" and not tracking that it depends on staying HSA-eligible through December 31, 2027.States the testing-period consequence -- taxable income plus a 10% additional tax if eligibility lapses early -- every time the last-month rule applies.
Matching the HDHP deductible/out-of-pocket bounds to the right coverage typeChecking a plan's deductible or out-of-pocket maximum against the wrong coverage type's 2026 figures (self-only vs. family), which can flip whether a plan reads as HDHP-qualified.Applies the 2026 self-only or family bounds you selected -- deductible ≥ $1,700/$3,400, out-of-pocket ≤ $8,500/$17,000 -- to the same coverage type as the contribution limit.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

Worked example: family coverage, 6 of 12 months eligible, age 55+

This is the calculator's own shipped "load example" scenario -- open the calculator and click it to see the same numbers.

QuantityCorrect (this calculator)Common hand-check error
Base limit (family, 6/12 months)$8,750.00 × 6/12 = $4,375.00$4,375.00 (same -- this step is usually done correctly)
Age-55 catch-up$1,000.00 × 6/12 = $500.00 (also prorated)$1,000.00 (left unprorated)
Total 2026 contribution limit$4,875.00$5,375.00 -- $500.00 too high

For comparison, the same coverage and age electing the last-month rule instead of proration (eligible on December 1, 2026) correctly totals $9,750.00 -- the full $8,750.00 family limit plus the full, unprorated $1,000.00 catch-up -- which is a different election with a testing-period condition attached, not a bigger version of the proration mistake above.

Common questions

Is the age-55 catch-up prorated the same way as the base HSA limit?

Yes, under the ordinary monthly-proration method -- and this is the step a manual check most often skips. The $1,000 catch-up is fixed by statute rather than adjusted for inflation, which reads as if it were a flat add-on regardless of how many months you were eligible. It isn't: for someone eligible 6 of 12 months, the catch-up itself is prorated to $500, on top of the prorated base limit. A hand calculation that adds the full $1,000 catch-up to a correctly prorated base limit overstates the total by the unprorated portion of the catch-up.

What's the most common way a manual proration ends up wrong?

Prorating the base limit correctly and then adding the full, unprorated age-55 catch-up on top of it. For family coverage with 6 eligible months and the catch-up, the correct total is $4,875 ($4,375 base plus a prorated $500 catch-up) -- a hand check that forgets to prorate the catch-up lands on $5,375 instead, $500 too high.

Why would someone contribute the full annual limit under the last-month rule instead of the prorated amount?

Because the last-month rule is a genuine, separate election, not a rounding shortcut: anyone HSA-eligible on December 1 of the tax year may contribute the full annual limit even if eligible for only part of the year, catch-up included at its full, unprorated amount. It is not the same total as a proration mistake that happens to look similar -- it is the correct total for a real election that comes with its own separate condition, the testing period below.

What is easy to miss about the last-month rule's testing period when checking it by hand?

That the extra amount is conditional, not final, until the testing period ends. Electing the last-month rule requires staying HSA-eligible through December 31 of the following year. If eligibility lapses before then for a reason other than death or disability, the amount contributed beyond what ordinary proration would have allowed becomes taxable income in the year eligibility lapsed, plus a 10% additional tax. A hand check that stops at "I get the full limit this year" and never carries the condition forward has only computed half the rule.

Does checking my own HDHP deductible and out-of-pocket maximum by hand carry the same risk?

It has its own separate failure point: mixing up the self-only and family bounds. For 2026 the deductible floor is $1,700 self-only versus $3,400 family, and the out-of-pocket ceiling is $8,500 self-only versus $17,000 family -- a plan checked against the wrong coverage type's bounds can read as HDHP-qualified when it isn't, or the reverse.
